query: For multiprincipal-element alloys intended for sustained use in harsh high-temperature environments, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs oxidation resistance and material integrity, and why? Define a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing behavior, the observations predicted relative to a baseline, the range over which the hypothesis should hold, relevant supporting evidence, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In refractory multiprincipal-element alloys (RHEAs) the long-term oxidation resistance and retention of mechanical integrity at ≥1000 °C are governed by whether a continuous, slow-growing Al2O3 surface scale forms; this occurs only when the alloy’s bulk Al activity exceeds a threshold that supports selective Al oxidation faster than the competitive formation of volatile, non-protective Mo/W oxides. When the threshold is met, Al2O3 acts as the primary diffusion barrier, minimizes mass gain, and arrests subsurface depletion so that the matrix maintains its strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Baseline alloy: equiatomic MoNbTaW (single-phase BCC, grain size 20–50 µm).
generation.intervention: Add 8–12 at.% Al at the expense of Mo and W to prepare Mo0.20Nb0.20Ta0.20W0.20Al0.20 (or comparable) while keeping processing history identical (vacuum arc melting, homogenization 1400 °C/24 h, identical surface finish).
generation.conditions: Static air at 1100 °C for 100 h (and confirm at 900 °C and 1200 °C to establish range).
generation.structural_mediator: Development (or absence) of a continuous, adherent α-Al2O3 external scale formed by selective outward diffusion and oxidation of Al.
generation.mechanism: If Al activity is above the critical level, Al oxidizes preferentially and the resulting dense Al2O3 layer blocks inward O2 and outward metal diffusion (parabolic kinetics, kp ≲ 1×10⁻⁸ g² cm⁻⁴ s⁻¹). The barrier suppresses formation/evaporation of MoO3 and WO3, limits internal oxidation, and preserves the BCC matrix, thereby retaining hardness and creep strength. Below the activity threshold, mixed porous (Mo,W)-oxides form, spall, and accelerate degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Al-containing alloy will show (a) total mass gain ≤1 mg cm⁻² after 100 h—at least a factor of 5–10 lower than the baseline, (b) parabolic rate constant kp at least one order of magnitude smaller, (c) a single, 2–4 µm thick, continuous Al2O3 layer with minimal internal oxidation depth (<1 µm) and no detectable MoO3 spallation; baseline alloy will exhibit >10 mg cm⁻² mass gain, non-protective multilayer oxides, and grain-boundary attack.
generation.baseline: MoNbTaW alloy with 0 at.% Al under the same thermal exposure.
generation.boundary: Expected to hold for 900–1200 °C in atmospheres with pO₂ ≳10⁻⁴ atm and for grain sizes ≤100 µm; will break down if Al content <~8 at.% or if silicon, boron, or melt impurities disrupt continuous Al2O3 formation.
generation.uncertainty: Exact Al activity threshold and the influence of Cr or Si additions are uncertain; possible competitive Cr2O3 formation may modify the scale. Quantitative kp values may vary with surface finish.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare coupons of baseline and Al-modified alloys, polish to 1 µm finish, weigh (±0.01 mg), expose them simultaneously in a horizontal tube furnace with flowing lab air at 1100 °C for 100 h. Record mass at 1, 10, 30, and 100 h; characterize surfaces and cross-sections by XRD, SEM/EDS, and FIB-TEM for scale continuity.
measurements: Mass change per unit area vs time
Microhardness or nanoindentation of subsurface matrix
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-containing alloy does NOT show (i) at least 5× lower mass gain than the baseline OR (ii) lacks a continuous Al2O3 scale (≥90 % surface coverage) after 100 h, the hypothesis is falsified.
